full_query: A 36-year-old G3P2002 woman presents to her obstetrician’s office for her 1st prenatal visit at 10 weeks and 2 days gestation. She has felt nauseous the last several mornings and has been tired for a few weeks. The patient has had 2 uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal deliveries at full term with her last child born 6 years ago. She is concerned about the risk of Down syndrome in this fetus, as her sister gave birth to an affected child at age 43. She has a history of generalized anxiety disorder, atopic dermatitis, and she is currently on escitalopram. Her temperature is 98.6°F (37.0°C), pulse is 70/min, blood pressure is 121/67 mmHg, and respirations are 13/min. The patient appears anxious, but overall comfortable, and cardiopulmonary and abdominal exams are unremarkable. Pelvic exam reveals normal external genitalia, a closed and soft cervix, a 10-week-sized uterus, and no adnexal masses. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for definitively determining whether this patient’s fetus has Down syndrome? (A) Amniocentesis (B) Anatomy ultrasound (C) Chorionic villus sampling (D) Genetic testing of patient’s sister (E) Nuchal translucency test

snippets.output: The patient, a 36‑year‑old woman with a history of generalized anxiety disorder on escitalopram, is 10 weeks and 2 days pregnant, has a normal physical and pelvic exam, and is concerned about Down syndrome due to a family history in which her sister had a child with Down syndrome at age 43.

Options for definitive diagnosis of Down syndrome in this pregnancy include amniocentesis, anatomy ultrasound, chorionic villus sampling, genetic testing of the patient’s sister, and nuchal translucency test.
Amniocentesis is an invasive diagnostic test performed between 15 and 20 weeks of gestation and can confirm the presence of Down syndrome.
An anatomy ultrasound is used for anatomical survey at about 18 to 20 weeks of gestation and can detect structural anomalies.
Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) is an invasive diagnostic procedure that can be performed between 10 and 13 weeks of gestation and can definitively diagnose Down syndrome.
Genetic testing of the patient’s sister would not inform the status of the current pregnancy and is therefore irrelevant to diagnosing fetal Down syndrome.
A nuchal translucency test is conducted between 11 and 14 weeks of gestation; it is a screening test that can suggest the risk of trisomy 21 but does not provide a definitive diagnosis.

Only invasive procedures such as amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling provide a definitive diagnosis of Down syndrome. At 10 weeks and 2 days gestation, chorionic villus sampling is suitable because it can be performed from the 10th week, whereas amniocentesis is typically performed later and would not be appropriate at this stage.
